OUR PRODUCTION
We primarily adopt an in-house manufacturing model, supplemented by a minor portion of
subcontracted processing for specific non-core processes. Our production strategy is distinctly
categorized. For standard products, including drill bits and milling cutters, we operate under a make-to-
stock approach driven by market demand. Our Supply Management & Planning Department develops
both annual and monthly production schedules accordingly, while remaining agile to make real-time
adjustments in response to fluctuating market demands and inventory levels, thereby ensuring an
effective balance between planning flexibility and structured execution. Conversely, for products like
grinding and polishing materials and intelligent CNC tools, we typically employ a make-to-order model,
initiating production upon the confirmation of customer orders. Throughout all processes, the Quality
Department rigorously adheres to the quality management system, implementing effective controls over
the quality of raw materials, semi-finished and finished products to guarantee product consistency,
stability and compliance with customer delivery requirements.
We have synergistically integrated digital-intelligent manufacturing, intelligent warehousing and
flexible production to build a smart manufacturing system that entails fully automated production lines,
advanced quality-control systems and an end-to-end process-visibility intelligent platform.
. Advanced automation and real time quality control. For our core drill bits, our end-to-end
automation exceeds 90%, enabling continuous quality monitoring and automated material
delivery. Each drill bit carries a unique serial code to enable unit-level serialization and full
life-cycle traceability from production, in-plant transfer through to application. With our self-
developed automated optical inspection deployed across the line to measure critical
dimensions in real time. Dimensional tolerances are controlled within 0.002 mm and
automatic equipment compensation is triggered as needed.
. Intelligent warehousing and logistics. We operate an automated storage and retrieval system
with autonomous guided vehicles for line-side storage. Line-side inbound and outbound
operations and inventory counting are executed by system-scheduled automation. This has
improved warehouse efficiency and reduced picking labor costs. Our warehouse management
system (WMS) is seamlessly integrated with enterprise resource planning (ERP) to assign
storage locations by outbound orders, optimize picking routes and enforce accurate first-in,
first-out control.

. Flexible production and supplier connectivity. Through optimized equipment layouts and
modular fixture/tooling design, we achieve rapid specification changeovers and dynamically
generate optimal production sequences based on order mix and equipment status. We also
maintain data links with raw-material suppliers to align just-in-time deliveries with
production plans and lower inventory occupation.
We regularly upgrade machinery, perform routine and preventive maintenance and optimize
production technologies to improve efficiency and product quality. Our production process is designed
to maintain consistent quality while preserving flexibility to expedite delivery. See ‘‘— Research and

In addition, we have our self-designed and built in-house tools for our manufacturing. For
example, our DTGM2200 High-Precision Five-Axis CNC Tool Grinder (the ‘‘DTGM2200’’) is our
innovative five-axis CNC tool grinder featuring multi-axis linkage control and full closed-loop motion
and a direct-drive rotary axis. In combination with a numeral system and Renishaw in-process probing,
it enables precise clamping, real-time measurement and automatic compensation, supporting stable
geometries and repeatable accuracy. Its dual grinding-wheel group accommodates up to six wheels
concurrently, reducing changeover time and enabling efficient production of complex profiles. The
DTGM2200 is deployed on our production lines for the precision grinding of milling tools, drilling tools
and forming tools across a wide diameter range, including micro-diameters, thereby improving
throughput, shortening setup cycles and enhancing yield under SPC-managed process control.

LOGISTICS
In terms of logistics and delivery, we adopt a combination of door-to-door delivery by our own
vehicle fleet and third-party logistics services. For customers in the Pearl River Delta region, we
generally use our own fleet to provide door-to-door delivery services, while for customers outside
Guangdong Province, we primarily rely on third-party logistics service providers given their more
favorable logistics cost structure. We engage qualified third-party logistics service providers for the
delivery of finished products from our production facilities to locations specified by our customers. Save
as provided in certain arrangement, we generally assume responsibility for logistics and the related
expenses. We set strict standards for the transportation of our products that these third-party logistics
service providers are required to follow and we evaluate the third-party logistics service providers on
their compliance and performance to ensure smooth delivery of products to customers. Through ongoing
enhancements, we are consistently improving delivery timeliness, accuracy and customer satisfaction
while achieving cost reductions. To the best of our knowledge, all of these logistics service providers
are Independent Third Parties.
During the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, we had not experienced any
significant delay or inappropriate handling of goods that materially and adversely affected our business
operations.
INVENTORY MANAGEMENT
Our inventories consist of raw materials, work in progress and finished goods. We currently store
all our inventories in warehouses in our production facilities in Dongguan and Nanyang. For raw
materials supplied by suppliers, we generally keep an inventory that would satisfy our production needs,
which may vary according to the demand of our customers, sales and production plans.
VMI warehouses
We provide inbound logistics services centered on a VMI warehouse model, which combines
coordinated collection and delivery arrangements with just-in-time fulfillment models with VMI
warehouse management, optimizing inventory levels to better match production demand. Unlike the
traditional supplier-to-factory model, where suppliers dispatch materials directly to factories based on
short-term demand signals, our VMI warehouse model allows for more proactive and coordinated supply
chain planning and more closely and responsively aligns inventory level with actual demand.
– 145 –

=== PAGE 156 ===
BUSINESS
Within the VMI warehouses, we perform incoming quality inspections and material preprocessing
(such as cutting or treatment as needed), tracing materials via batch identification. This enables the
direct delivery of production-ready materials to factories, streamlining in-factory operations, freeing up
line-side floor space, reducing line-side inventory and in-plant material movements, supporting quicker
changeovers and higher line utilization, and reducing lead times.

The number of customers with VMI arrangements and the revenue contribution from such

RMB1,155.0 million in 2025, primarily attributable to higher procurement volumes from several major
existing customers under VMI arrangements as these customers increased their use of VMI arrangements
to support their production scheduling, inventory management and just-in-time supply needs.
Under our VMI arrangements, (i) products stored at VMI warehouses generally remain owned by
us prior to being withdrawn for use, and title typically transfers when such products are withdrawn for
use on the customer’s production line; (ii) customers generally conduct receipt procedures and quality
inspections upon arrival and manage the storage and withdrawal of such products in accordance with
agreed inventory management principles, such as first-in-first-out; (iii) the relevant customer is generally
responsible for the safekeeping of inventory and bears the risk of loss, theft, damage or shrinkage of
such inventory while it remains in the VMI warehouse; (iv) we remain responsible for product quality
defects or non-conformity; and (v) settlement is generally determined by reference to actual withdrawals
or consumption with periodic reconciliation. Our Directors are of the view that the risk of material
returns of drill bit inventory under our VMI arrangements is relatively low, as such arrangements are
typically adopted by customers to support production scheduling and secure continuity of supply, and
customers generally have limited commercial incentive to return drill bit inventory maintained at VMI
warehouses other than in circumstances involving product quality issues or other agreed contractual
grounds.
Inventory management
Our current inventory level of raw materials can support the ongoing manufacturing activities,
among which metal materials are usually kept at an inventory level of fewer than three months. We
manage our inventory level by considering factors including but not limited to sales forecasts,
production cycles, procurement cycles, number of suppliers, purchase price subject to purchase scale and
future trend of purchase prices, instead of depending on the nature of raw materials. We have procedures
in place to monitor the aforementioned factors on a regular basis to ensure the inventory level of raw
materials is able to support relevant production schedules. In addition, these raw materials are not scarce
materials and can be readily procured from a variety of suppliers. We believe our current inventory level
of raw materials is able to satisfy our ongoing manufacturing needs.
All our products are subject to expiry. Different products carry different recommended storage
periods and are subject to shelf-life controls. As a general guideline, our finished products generally
have recommended storage periods ranging from approximately three to ten years, depending on their
product type, nature and storage conditions. By way of example, our drill bits have a recommended
– 146 –

BUSINESS
storage period of approximately ten years under proper storage. We regularly monitor our inventories to
reduce the risk of overstocking. We have in place internal policies which require a physical count of all
our raw materials, work in progress and finished goods once every half year to identify products that are
damaged, expired or soon-to-be expired.
Our Directors confirmed that our inventory control policies have been effective and we did not
experience any material shortage in supply or overstocking of inventories during the Track Record
Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date.
As of December 31, 2023, 2024 and 2025, our inventories amounted to RMB339.8 million,
RMB389.1 million and RMB580.0 million, respectively.

Channel Partners
We also engage channel partners, who are mainly third-party partners that procure our products
from us, perform simple processing on such products and then sell them to end customers as part of the
channel partners’ own offerings. For our functional film materials, such processing typically involves
basic operations such as cutting, slitting or repackaging to meet specific size, format or application
requirements of particular projects, without altering the essential properties or specifications of the
underlying materials. In some cases, these channel partners also assist us with customer development
and the coordination of end customers’ requirements for our functional film materials. The end
customers served by our channel partners are generally manufacturers and other industry participants
that use functional film materials in their production processes.
We generally enter into the same form of sales and purchase agreements with our channel partners
as with our other direct customers, on substantially the same salient terms. The salient terms of the sales
and purchase agreements between us and our channel partners are set out below.
. Product specifications. Our channel partners typically procure functional film materials from
us.
. Pricing policy. We sell our products to channel partners at price agreed with the channel
partners.
. Logistics. We are responsible for delivering our products to locations agreed with our
channel partners.
. Transfer of risks. The risks transfer to channel partners after they complete the inspection
and confirm the receipt of our products.
. Return arrangements. We typically do not allow our channel partners to return products to
us except for limited reasons, such as product design defects or quality issues.
. Warranty. We typically offer channel partners a 12-month product warranty.
We do not impose any sales targets on our channel partners and we do not conduct any tender
process for the appointment of channel partners. The number of our channel partners was 22, 18 and 14
in 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively. In 2023, 2024 and 2025, revenue generated from channel partners
was RMB65.4 million, RMB108.4 million and RMB28.3 million, respectively, accounting for 5.1%,
7.0% and 1.4% for the respective years.
Although a portion of our customers are channel partners rather than end customers, our Directors
are of the view that our business model does not constitute a distributorship model. As stated above, our
channel partners are not our distributors that we engage to broaden our sales channels. They are
generally our integrated channel partners selected by our end customers to procure functional film
materials. After our channel partners receive products from us, they generally perform light processing

Agents
In addition to direct sales and sales through channel partners, we also sell our products through
agents. Our agents are Independent Third Parties with whom we have entered into standing agent
agreements under which they promote and sell our products to end customers in designated regions or
for specified customer segments. We generally regard these agents as an extension of our sales network
and an important supplement to our direct sales efforts in markets where we do not maintain a full on-
the-ground presence. We maintain a buyer-seller relationship with our agents.
We sell our products to agents, who in turn generally sell such products to corporate end
customers within predetermined geographic areas or specified customer segments, primarily end users of
our specialized PCB production equipment. We do not appoint any sub-agents and do not enter into any
contractual arrangements with any sub-agents in connection with the sale of our products. We carefully
select our agents based on a range of factors, including industry experience, customer coverage, sales
execution capability, ability to meet agreed growth targets, creditworthiness and service quality. In the
ordinary course of business, we may terminate relationships with agents for various commercial reasons,
including where our expansion plans and sales strategy have outgrown the sales capacity or geographic
focus of certain agents.

Major terms of our standard agent agreements with our agents include:

from our agents. We only allow product exchanges under limited circumstances such as
quality defects or damages during transportation.
. Termination. We are entitled to terminate the agent agreements if our agents breach the agent
agreements.

We believe that the risk of channel stuffing in respect of our sales to agents is low, based on the
following factors: (i) our relationship with agents is a buyer-seller relationship and agents are
responsible for their own inventory risks; (ii) we generally do not accept returns of products from agents
and only permit exchanges under limited circumstances such as quality defects or transportation damage;
and (iii) during the Track Record Period, revenue generated from sales to agents accounted for less than
5% of our total revenue for each period, such that any adverse impact arising from potential channel
stuffing at the agent level would not be expected to have a material effect on our overall revenue. We do
not set minimum purchase targets or sales goals for our agents. Our agents are responsible for their own
inventory risks. Accordingly, we do not require our agents to maintain a minimum inventory level.
We manage our agents through order and settlement management, marketing support, training and
evaluation. Our relationship with agents is a standard buyer-seller relationship, and we consider agents
to be our customers, who further sell our products to end users of our specialized PCB production
equipment. Our sales team evaluates agents based on, among other things, their sales performance,
financial and credit status and cooperation in sales network development. We monitor agent performance
on an ongoing basis, including sales performance, customer feedback and compliance with our policies.
Where issues are identified, such as under-performance, non-compliance or conduct that may adversely
affect our brand or customer relationships, we may take remedial actions, including enhanced
supervision, restriction of scope or termination of the relevant agency relationship.
Mitigation of cannibalization risk among sales channels
We sell our products through three main sales channels, namely (i) direct sales to end customers,
(ii) sales to channel partners and (iii) sales through agents. While multiple sales channels may give rise
to potential channel conflict or cannibalization, we manage such risk through the following measures:
Channel management and avoidance of overlap. As described above, we deploy different sales
channels depending on customer needs and commercial circumstances. We implement scope controls and
ongoing monitoring for our agent arrangements, and require the relevant parties to coordinate on a
timely basis to identify and resolve potential overlap, including aligning the applicable channel and
commercial terms for the same customer opportunity.
Ongoing monitoring and channel discipline. Our channel partners and agents are managed by us
based on regional market dynamics. We monitor channel performance and customer feedback on an
ongoing basis and, take remedial actions (including enhanced supervision, restriction of scope or
termination) to maintain channel discipline and minimize channel overlap.
Based on the above, our Directors are of the view that our measures to manage potential
cannibalization among our sales channels are adequate and effective. Nothing has come to the Joint
Sponsors’ attention that would disagree with the Directors’ view above.
Pricing
We price our products based on factors including prices of competing products, costs of raw
materials and consumables, cost of production, market position of the product as well as expected
purchase orders. For high-end products, we also consider the need for maintaining the premium status of
our brands and high-end products. Our final quotation is determined based on the reasonable range of
gross profit margin generated by the pricing process. All pricing requires internal approval through
customer evaluation and credit review processes.

Sales and Marketing
We have a strong and dedicated sales team, consisting of over 100 sales personnel as of December
31, 2025. Our key sales personnel, maintain close relationships and communication with our customers
through regular visits. To further enhance our sales and marketing capabilities, we conduct regular
training on the latest market developments and sales techniques. This initiative provides our sales team
with a comprehensive understanding of the market, improving market coverage and fostering a more
cohesive workforce.
We emphasize on collaborative R&D with customers who possess top-tier technical expertise and
significant global influence. Our R&D team engages in regular discussion with these customers to
explore the anticipated changes in their future products and the corresponding changes we need to make
to our process equipment. In this way, we ensure the compatibility between our equipment and their
standards, maintaining our future competitiveness. Thus, we maintain a close relationship with our
customers that goes far beyond a mere transactional relationship.
After-Sales Services
We believe that accessible, high-quality after-sales services are an important factor in customers’
purchase decisions. We provide full-lifecycle value-added services to support customers and enhance
customer loyalty and brand image.
Our equipment typically comes with a twelve-month warranty, while certain components of this
equipment may have a six-month warranty. After this period, free consultation for maintenance and
repair is available, but we charge fees for services including on-site confirmation, repair, and
replacement parts. As part of our full lifecycle value-added services, we offer preventive maintenance
services at a charge, reinforcing the ‘‘maintain, not repair’’ philosophy and helping customers improve
operational efficiency and reduce costs.
We regularly conduct professional and technical training to improve the professional skills of after-
sales service personnel. To ensure the quality of our after-sales services, we conduct regular appraisals
with regards to their performance. We have also appointed designated chief service officer for some of
our customers to coordinate value-added services across all equipment categories, offering bespoke
solutions tailored to customer’s specific on-site processes and production conditions. These solutions
include automation recommendations, capacity and quality enhancement, as well as precision
improvements for old products.
When a complaint arises, our team typically visits the customer’s site to thoroughly understand the
context and determine the cause of the problem. Additionally, we pass on customers’ emerging needs to
our product centers to offer innovative solutions for customers. We also conduct return visits to ensure
customer satisfaction.
In terms of return and exchange of our consumable products such as drill bits, milling cutters,
grinding and polishing materials, and functional film materials, we outline all specifications of the
products before signing contracts with customers. Upon delivery, our products are inspected against each
specification. In case it is determined that some specifications are not satisfied, we address the defects
through repair, upgrade or restoration. If any batch is identified as non-conforming within the agreed
acceptance window, we arrange replacement or exchange. We typically do not allow our direct
customers or channel partners to return products to us except for limited reasons, such as product design
defects or quality issues. We also typically do not accept returns or exchanges of products from our
agents, and only allow exchanges under limited circumstances such as quality defects or damage during
transportation. Although we recorded certain product returns in the ordinary course of business during
the Track Record Period, such returns were immaterial. The amount of product returns, measured by the
sales value of returned products, was RMB3.1 million, RMB6.5 million and RMB11.3 million in 2023,

Third-Party Payment Arrangements
Background of Third-Party Payment Arrangements
Historically, some of our customers (individually or collectively, the ‘‘Relevant Customers’’)
settled their payments with our Group through accounts of third-party payors designated by these
Relevant Customers at their requests (the ‘‘Third-Party Payment Arrangement(s)’’). During the Track
Record Period, third-party payors designated by the Relevant Customers primarily included the Relevant
Customers’ legal representative, business partners, etc. Our Directors have confirmed that none of the
third party payors designated by the Relevant Customers during the Track Record Period is a connected
person of our Group and such designated third-party payors are independent from any of our Group’s
Directors, senior management and Shareholders. See ‘‘Risk Factors — Risks Relating to Our Business
and Industry — We are subject to risks relating to third-party payments.’’
In 2023, 2024 and 2025, a total number of two, two and one Relevant Customers utilized the
Third-Party Payment Arrangements to settle payments with us, respectively. The aggregate amount of
payments from their designated third-party payors was RMB21.1 thousand, RMB67.9 thousand and
RMB265 in 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively, representing approximately 0.002%, 0.004% and nil of
our revenue, respectively. The amount settled through Third Party Payment Arrangements only
accounted for a small portion of our total revenue for each period of the Track Record Period.
Throughout the Track Record Period, no individual Relevant Customer in China made a material
contribution to our revenue.
During the Track Record Period, we implemented internal control measures to monitor and manage
the Third-Party Payment Arrangements. We typically required all Relevant Customers and their
designated third-party payers to provide us with written letters of undertaking (the ‘‘Undertaking
Letters’’) prior to making payments under the Third-Party Payment Arrangements. The Undertaking
Letters generally specified that the designated third-party payer was authorized to settle payments with
us on behalf of the Relevant Customers through pre-agreed accounts of such designated third-party
payers, and that all activities conducted through such pre-agreed accounts would constitute activities of
the Relevant Customers, for which the Relevant Customers would assume full responsibility. To verify
the authenticity of the Third-Party Payment Arrangements, our finance personnel were authorized to
recognize only payments received from designated third-party payers of the Relevant Customers, and
our business personnel were permitted to deliver our products to the Relevant Customers only on the
condition that the information of the designated third-party payers matched that set out in the
corresponding Undertaking Letters. Based on the foregoing, our Directors believe that the Third-Party
Payment Arrangements during the Track Record Period were, to the best of their knowledge and belief,
completely and accurately recorded in our accounting books and records in all material respects.

All such Third-Party Payment Arrangements were fully traceable, as each payment could be
matched to the Relevant Customers, the underlying sales transaction and the Undertaking Letter or other

third-party payers to facilitate or incentivize the Third-Party Payment Arrangements. All Third-Party
Payment Arrangements were initiated by the Relevant Customers, rather than by us, and the relevant

In addition, we received limited inadvertent Third-Party Payment Arrangements at our German
Subsidiary from certain legacy customers of MPK in connection with the post-acquisition transition of
the relevant business in 2025. Such payments arose primarily because such customers continued to remit
payments based on their historical payment practices and administrative habits. The aggregate amount of
such payments during the Track Record Period was approximately EUR100,000, representing only an
immaterial portion of our revenue.
Reasons for Third-Party Payment Arrangements
To the best of our knowledge, the Relevant Customers requested to utilize the Third-Party Payment
Arrangements to settle payments with us for their own convenience and flexibility. These Relevant
Customers commonly opted for settlements through corporate or personal accounts held by designated
third-party payors, such as the Relevant Customers’ affiliated companies and shareholders. As confirmed
by Frost & Sullivan, it is not uncommon for customers to use third-party payors to settle corporate
transactions with their suppliers due to convenience and flexibility.
Legal Consequences of Third-Party Payment Arrangements
Our PRC Legal Advisor is of the view that, based on the information and explanations we have
provided, (i) the payment form adopted under our Third-Party Payment Arrangements during the Track
Record Period did not violate the mandatory provisions of PRC laws and administrative regulations, (ii)
the likelihood that we would, as a result of such arrangements, be found to constitute unjust enrichment
under the Civil Code of the PRC and be required to return amounts already paid is low, and (iii) the risk
that our mere receipt of payments for goods under such arrangements would be deemed to constitute
money laundering under the PRC Criminal Law is low. In addition, we were not subject to any material
administrative penalties by the PRC tax authorities in respect of such arrangements during the Track
Record Period.
Based on the follow-up review of the implementation of these measures, our Directors are of the
view that these measures are effective and adequate in preventing unauthorized Third-Party Payment
Arrangements and the associated risks.
Cessation of Third-Party Payment Arrangements
We have substantially rectified and ceased third-party payment arrangements in the ordinary course
of business and do not intend to enter into any new or intentional third-party payment arrangements
going forward. Based on (i) the very limited number of Relevant Customers involved, (ii) the immaterial
historical amount settled through the Third-Party Payment Arrangements, which represented less than
0.01% of our revenue in each year of the Track Record Period, (iii) the fact that no individual Relevant
– 155 –

=== PAGE 166 ===
BUSINESS
Customer made a material contribution to our revenue, and (iv) the fact that the Third-Party Payment
Arrangements were requested by the Relevant Customers for settlement convenience and were not
essential to our ability to collect trade receivables, our Directors are of the view that the cessation of the
Third-Party Payment Arrangements would not have a material adverse effect on our operations, liquidity
or financial performance. The Joint Sponsors, having made due and reasonable enquiries, are of the view
that nothing has come to their attention that would cause them to disagree with the Directors’ view.
Notwithstanding the foregoing, limited inadvertent Third-Party Payment Arrangements may
continue to occur in the near term at our German Subsidiary in isolated cases due to certain legacy
customers’ historical remittance practices following the acquisition of the MPK business.
Internal Control Measures
To implement our planned cessation of the Third-Party Payment Arrangements and mitigate the
associated risks, we have adopted a Third-Party Collection and Payment Policy setting out the relevant
governance, documentation and compliance requirements. As a general rule, all new orders must be
settled directly by customers from accounts in their own names. In exceptional circumstances where
direct payment is objectively not feasible, any Third-Party Payment Arrangement is subject to prior
approval under our written procedures, pursuant to which the relevant business unit must submit the
relevant supporting documents, including, where applicable, an executed tripartite agreement, the
underlying contract, agent qualification certificates and payment breakdown details, for review by our
finance and legal departments and approval by our general manager, and transactions exceeding RMB2
million require additional consideration by the general manager’s executive meeting; absent such
approval, payment must be made through the customer’s contractual account.
In addition, we maintain KYC and sanctions-screening procedures and our internal audit
department periodically reviews receipt records and supporting documents to verify payer backgrounds,
trace fund flows and match payments against the underlying sales contracts, with a view to preventing
misuse of third-party payments for improper purposes such as fraud, commercial bribery or money
laundering. Based on the follow-up review of the implementation of these measures, our Directors are of
the view that these measures are effective and adequate to implement the planned cessation of the Third-
Party Payment Arrangements, prevent recurrence and mitigate the associated legal and compliance risks.

QUALITY CONTROL
We maintain comprehensive policies, SOPs and work instructions to ensure product quality across
the full lifecycle. We are certified to ISO 9001, IATF 16949 and ISO 14001, and operate a dedicated
Quality Control Department led by senior management to oversee implementation and continuous
improvement. We have strengthened standardized production and quality management training, and
established a full lifecycle quality control system covering product R&D, supply chain, production
process and customer service. Our quality control measures include the following:
Raw Material Quality Control. We implement classified management and differential inspection
standards for raw materials, with a focus on verifying the composition and physical properties of key
materials such as tungsten steel. Strategic collaborative relationships are maintained with core suppliers
to ensure material quality and stability.
In-Process Quality Control. Automated inspection equipment and real-time monitoring systems are
deployed throughout the manufacturing process to maintain precision and consistency. A full-process
traceability system enables rapid identification and resolution of any quality deviations.
Finished Product Quality Control. We employ comprehensive inspection protocols, including
automated visual detection, to ensure all finished products meet established quality standards. Products
are categorized and managed based on inspection results, with non-conforming items handled through
structured review and disposal procedures.
– 158 –

=== PAGE 169 ===
BUSINESS
Customer-Oriented Quality Assurance. Our sales model allows strict control over delivery
process, with each batch accompanied by complete inspection data. We have established efficient
customer feedback mechanisms, typically resolving quality issues within one-to-two weeks through
standardized analysis and improvement processes.
SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT
Raw Materials and Procurement
The key raw materials we procure include tungsten carbide, stainless steel wire, film substrates,
brush plates and ceramic strips, etc.
We primarily procure raw materials in China. For the procurement of raw materials, we analyze the
timing and scheduling of raw material deliveries, taking into account factors such as the material
requirements planning, production scheduling, inventory safety, and supplier lead times. These plans can
be communicated to our suppliers, which will then execute deliveries according to our plans.
Potential pricing fluctuations in our raw materials can arise due to factors including global and
domestic economic conditions, governmental regulations, supply-demand dynamics and geopolitical
conditions. We generally adopt a one-time pricing model. The one-time pricing model sets a fixed price
during the term of a contract, providing certainty for both parties, and such prices are typically
determined through annual tendering processes and commercial negotiations. If market prices fluctuate,
we will re-confirm the agreed prices with the relevant suppliers and make corresponding adjustments as
appropriate.
During the Track Record Period, we experienced certain constraints in the supply of materials for
our functional film products. To address potential supply bottlenecks and reduce our reliance on external
suppliers, we have implemented an approach to progressively internalize the development and
production of core materials for our functional film business. In the meantime, we have continued to
expand our list of qualified alternative suppliers and to optimize and automate our production processes
to enhance capacity utilization and improve the overall operating efficiency of our functional film
business. See ‘‘Risk Factors — Risks Relating to Our Business and Industry — We may be unable to
effectively manage the supply, quality and pricing of our principal raw materials and components, and
supply shortages and price fluctuations could increase our costs and adversely affect our margins and
results of operations.’’
Supplier Selection and Management
We have established stringent management mechanisms for the selection and retention of suppliers.
In accordance with the supplier management policy, we conduct due diligence and select suppliers based
on the availability, price and quality of the services or products, delivery time, as well as the reputation,
credential and experience of the suppliers. Supplier qualifications are assessed through factory audits
and sample testing. Companies in the qualified supplier list are subject to regular evaluation and re-
assessment, in order to ensure their compliance with our policies and standards.
Our procurement methods include requests for quotation and agreements, and we select suitable
suppliers from the qualified supplier pool based on the nature of the raw materials. For standardized
components, procurement is primarily based on factors such as the quality, price, and delivery time of
the raw materials. For custom components, we select suppliers based on their technical expertise,
processing capabilities and quotations.
During the Track Record Period, we did not enter into any long-term supply agreements with our
suppliers that included fixed-price arrangements. In response to the potential raw material price
increases, we primarily mitigate the impact by building long-term relationships with our suppliers,
– 159 –

=== PAGE 170 ===
BUSINESS
maintaining close communication and conducting secondary source evaluations. Meanwhile, we conduct
R&D on new materials and engage new suppliers to maintain the flexibility to switch to alternative
materials or suppliers in the event of severe shortages or price volatility of certain raw materials. We
have implemented periodic reviews and internal mechanisms to monitor the price of our raw materials
by considering current stock levels, future sales and market trends.
We require all of our suppliers to comply with our internal supply management policies. We
communicate with suppliers regarding quality standards, and thoroughly inspect the products received to
ensure that they meet all the technical requirements set forth in our product designs. We may conduct
regular or ad hoc on-site inspections of suppliers, and require suppliers to remedy quality issues upon
notice. Upon receiving materials and products from suppliers, we retain the right to reject or return
based on our inspection and examination results, and suppliers are generally liable to us and our
customers for any product quality issues of our products caused by them. We also require our suppliers
to sign an ‘‘Anti-Bribery Transaction Agreement,’’ by which they undertake in writing to comply with
the ethical requirements set out in the agreement.
Our Directors confirm that our Group did not experience any material disruption, disputes or delay
in relation to supply by our suppliers during the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable
Date.
Agreements with Suppliers
The salient terms of the supply agreements between us and our suppliers are set out below:
. Product specifications. We specify the product name, specification, price, quantity, delivery
timeline, delivery location and other details in each purchase order we send to our suppliers.
. Pricing policy. The settled prices quoted to us shall be based on market conditions and stated
in the purchase orders prevail.
. Logistics. We are responsible for delivering our products to locations agreed with our direct
sales customers.
. Transfer of risks. The risks transfer to direct sales customers after they complete the
inspection and confirm the receipt of our products.
. Return arrangements. The suppliers are responsible for packaging and shall ensure
reasonable packaging and protection during transportation.
. Quality Guarantee. Products are typically accepted in accordance with our specifications, as
well as national, local and industry standards. We are entitled to return any defective raw
materials that do not meet the specifications, and the suppliers shall remedy the same,
including product return and replacement.
. Confidentiality. All confidential information provided by either party shall not be disclosed
to any third party without prior consent.
. Termination. The agreement can be terminated upon written notice of one party, in the event
of fraud, bankruptcy or material breach of the agreement of the other party.

OVERLAPPING OF MAJOR SUPPLIERS AND CUSTOMERS
Among our top five customers in each year during the Track Record Period, Customer G was also
our supplier, supplying milling cutters to us in 2023, 2024 and 2025. This overlap primarily arose from
our closed-loop tooling program, under which we procure used milling cutters and related tooling scrap
from certain customers for reconditioning and material recycling. In 2023, 2024 and 2025, our revenue
from top five customers who were also our suppliers was RMB61.6 million, RMB71.2 million and
RMB80.8 million, respectively, representing 4.8%, 4.6% and 3.9% of our total revenue in the same
years. In 2023, 2024 and 2025, our purchase amount from top five customers who were also our
suppliers was less than 0.1% of our total purchase amount in the same years, respectively.
Among our top five suppliers in each year during the Track Record Period, Supplier B was also
our customer. Supplier B mainly provided tungsten carbide to us, and we mainly provided our drilling
tools to Supplier B. This overlap primarily arose from Supplier B’s normal purchases from us and
constituted a negligible portion of our revenue for the same period. In 2023, 2024 and 2025, our
revenue from top five suppliers who were also our customers was nil, RMB581.4 thousand and nil,
representing nil, 0.04% and nil of our total revenue in the same years. During the same periods, our
purchases from Supplier B amounted to RMB49.4 million, RMB62.9 million and RMB97.2 million,
accounting for 6.9%, 6.6% and 7.2% of our total procurement amount, respectively.
According to Frost & Sullivan, such overlap is common, especially considering our leading market
position and market share, as well as the depth of our collaboration with a wide customer and supplier
base, which make it more common for our customers/suppliers to engage with us in both selling
products and services to and purchasing products and services from us. Our Directors confirmed that all
of our sales to and purchases from these overlapping customers and suppliers were conducted in the
ordinary course of business under normal commercial terms and on an arm’s-length basis, and these
overlapping customers and suppliers are Independent Third Parties. Our Directors affirm that the prices
of transactions with these overlapping customers and suppliers are comparable to those of similar

substantially similar to those of our other customers or suppliers.
RECENT REGULATION IN RELATION TO TARIFFS, EXPORT CONTROLS AND
SANCTIONS
International Sanctions
During the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date (the ‘‘Review Period’’), our
activities did not involve any conduct that resulted in material sanctions risks to the Relevant Persons.
We did not engage in any transactions or other activities during the Review Period involving Sanctioned
Targets or persons located in Sanctioned Countries that are subject to International Sanctions enacted by
potentially Relevant Jurisdictions, except for the two categories of transactions described below.
First, in 2024, we made two sales transactions delivered in the PRC to a customer located in Iran,
a Comprehensively Sanctioned Country (the ‘‘Iran Customer’’), with an aggregate transaction amount
of less than RMB20,000 (the ‘‘Iran Transactions’’). We are not aware of any use of U.S. dollars or any
other U.S. nexus in connection with the Iran Transactions. In particular, the Iran Transactions were not
denominated or settled in U.S. dollars, were not processed through U.S. financial institutions, did not
involve any U.S. persons, and did not involve U.S.-origin items, software or technology or any
shipment, export or re-export from the United States. According to our International Sanctions Advisor,
the Iran Transactions would not constitute a violation of U.S. primary sanctions in the absence of such
U.S. nexus. Nevertheless, given the payment arrangements for the Iran Transactions, including the use
of a personal account and a third-party payor, the possibility that U.S. authorities might consider
whether any indirect U.S. nexus existed in connection with the Iran Transactions cannot be completely
excluded. In particular, if the Iran Transactions were determined to have involved intermediate U.S.
dollar wire transfers or other activities involving U.S. financial institutions after delivery to the Iran
Customer, U.S. authorities could take the position that the transactions involved the causing of a
violation by a U.S. person. Moreover, even if U.S. authorities were to determine that the Iran
Transactions involved a U.S. nexus after delivery to the Iran Customer, any resulting penalties would
likely be minimal, taking into account the very limited number and value of the transactions, their
isolated nature and specific circumstances, the absence of repeated conduct, and the remedial measures
we have adopted, including policies and procedures to refrain from conducting future business with
counterparties in Sanctioned Countries or with Sanctioned Targets and to restrict the acceptance of
payments from third-party payors.
Second, during the Review Period, we engaged in transactions with (i) a customer and supplier that
was designated on the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (the ‘‘SDN List’’) at the
time of the relevant transactions, and (ii) another customer that was also designated on the SDN List at
the time of the relevant transactions (collectively, the ‘‘SDN Transactions’’). The SDN Transactions
were denominated and settled in RMB, were not processed through U.S. financial institutions, and did
not involve U.S. persons, U.S.-origin items, software or technology, U.S. dollars, or any shipment,
export or re-export from U.S.. Accordingly, as advised by our International Sanctions Advisor, the SDN
Transactions did not involve the requisite U.S. nexus necessary to satisfy the jurisdictional elements of a
violation of U.S. primary sanctions.
The Iran Transactions and the SDN Transactions did not implicate primary sanctions administered
by the United Kingdom, the European Union, Australia or Canada.
– 163 –

=== PAGE 174 ===
BUSINESS
Under current U.S. law and practice, ‘‘Secondary Sanctionable Activity’’ generally involves
material support for SDNs or significant involvement with specified regions or sectors in Sanctioned
Countries. The Iran Transactions and the SDN Transactions could, in certain circumstances, potentially
be viewed as conduct giving rise to secondary sanctions considerations under U.S. law. We have taken,
and will continue to take, remedial measures to mitigate the risk that such conduct could result in
significant penalties.
In particular, we have established, and will continue to maintain and enhance, policies and
procedures to comply with applicable International Sanctions with a view to mitigating the risks of
primary sanctions violations or Secondary Sanctionable Activity. We will not place or accept any new
orders from any customers or suppliers that are subject to International Sanctions, nor will we accept
any new orders from customers located in any Sanctioned Countries.
After the Latest Practicable Date, we fully terminated all SDN Transactions on May 20, 2026.
Accordingly, as of May 20, 2026, there were no ongoing SDN Transactions and no outstanding
contracts with the counterparties involved in the SDN Transactions.
During the Review Period, the SDN Transactions comprised (i) sales of drill bits to, and
procurement of rough-ground rods and tool-sharpening services from, one SDN counterparty; and (ii)
sales of drill bits and metal accessories to another SDN counterparty.
The sales to the SDN counterparties amounted to approximately RMB163,900, RMB95,100 and
RMB93,300 in 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively, representing approximately 0.0001%, less than
0.0001% and less than 0.0001% of our total revenue for the respective years. The purchases from the
SDN counterparty amounted to approximately RMB31,200, RMB134,200 and RMB3.4 million in 2023,
2024 and 2025, respectively, representing approximately 0.004%, 0.01% and 0.3% of our total purchases
for the respective years.
Given the limited transaction amounts and their immaterial contribution to our revenue and
purchases during the Track Record Period, and taking into account that all SDN Transactions had been
fully terminated as of May 20, 2026, we do not expect the cessation of the SDN Transactions to have a
material adverse impact on our financial performance. As there were no outstanding contracts in respect
of the SDN Transactions as of May 20, 2026, there were no potential financial losses arising from non-
completion of existing contracts with the relevant SDN counterparties.
In addition, we have established, and will continue to maintain and regularly update customer and
supplier information in a systematic manner sufficient to enable verification of the identity of all new
customers and suppliers against Sanctioned Targets, including SDNs. We will also conduct periodic
sanctions screening of existing customers and suppliers on an ongoing basis.
U.S. authorities could view our gradual wind-down of business with the counterparties involved in
the SDN Transactions by the end of 2026 less favourably than an immediate termination. However, in
the absence of Primary Sanctions violations, the Company may have reasonable commercial and legal
grounds for the nine-month wind down (as further particularized above), which would ultimately
comport with the goals of the relevant U.S. sanctions programs.
In light of relevant published enforcement precedent and regulatory guidance, the risks that the
Company might become subject to Secondary Sanctions under U.S. law based on the Iran Transactions
and the SDN Transactions also are likely remote.

U.S. Export Controls and Tariff
The Export Administration Regulations (the ‘‘EAR’’) regulate U.S. export controls, and the Bureau
of Industry and Security (the ‘‘BIS’’) of the U.S. Department of Commerce administers the EAR. The
EAR regulate the export, re-export and in-country transfer of certain items, including U.S.-origin
products, software and technology, as well as certain non-U.S.-origin items that are otherwise subject to
the EAR. Under the EAR, licensing requirements applicable to parties on the BIS Entity List are
generally triggered only where the relevant transaction involves items subject to the EAR.
For non-U.S.-origin items, the key bases on which such items may become subject to the EAR
include, among others, the de minimis rule and the Foreign Direct Product Rules (the ‘‘FDPRs’’). Under
the de minimis rule, a foreign-made item may become subject to the EAR if it incorporates controlled
U.S.-origin commodities, software or technology above the applicable de minimis thresholds. Separately,
under the FDPRs, a foreign-produced item may become subject to the EAR if it is the direct product of
specified U.S.-origin technology or software, or is produced by a plant or major component of a plant
that itself is the direct product of specified U.S.-origin technology or software.
Our principal products comprise precision cutting tools, including drill bits, milling cutters and
specialized PCB tools, grinding and polishing materials, functional film materials and intelligent CNC
equipment used primarily in PCB fabrication and related precision manufacturing processes. These
products are mechanical tools, consumables, materials or equipment used in PCB drilling, routing,
surface treatment, planarization and related fabrication stages.
Our products are not U.S.-origin items, are not listed on the U.S. Commerce Control List (the
‘‘CCL’’) and are not specially designed for military, intelligence, nuclear, missile or other controlled
end uses. In particular, our products do not satisfy the technical descriptions of precision machinery
classifiable under Export Control Classification Numbers (‘‘ECCNs’’) 2B001 or 2B002.
Our products do not incorporate controlled U.S.-origin commodities, software or technology above
the applicable de minimis thresholds. In addition, our products are not the direct product of specified
U.S.-origin technology or software, and are not produced by any plant or major component of a plant
that itself is the direct product of specified U.S.-origin technology or software. In particular, our
manufacturing operations in China, Thailand and Germany do not rely on controlled U.S.-origin
technology or software, and do not utilize controlled semiconductor manufacturing equipment or
electronic design automation (‘‘EDA’’) software that would cause the relevant products to satisfy the
applicable FDPR product-scope requirements. On this basis, our International Sanctions Advisor is of
the view that our products are not expected to be subject to the EAR under the de minimis rule or the
FDPRs.
During the Review Period, we had historical transactions with one customer that was designated on
the BIS Entity List with Entity List Footnote 4 at the time of certain relevant transactions (the ‘‘Entity
List Customer’’). Entity List Footnote 4 expands the scope of the Entity List FDPR for certain foreign-
produced items involving relevant Entity List parties. However, Entity List Footnote 4 does not
automatically apply to all foreign-produced items supplied to such parties. Rather, it applies only where
the relevant foreign-produced item satisfies the applicable product-scope requirements, including that the
item is the direct product of specified U.S.-origin technology or software, or is produced by a plant or
major component of a plant that itself is the direct product of specified U.S.-origin technology or
software.
As discussed above, the products supplied by us to the Entity List Customer were not U.S.-origin
items, were not listed on the CCL, did not incorporate controlled U.S.-origin content above the
applicable de minimis thresholds, and did not satisfy the product-scope requirements under any
applicable FDPR, including the Entity List FDPR associated with Entity List Footnote 4. Accordingly,
– 165 –

BUSINESS
notwithstanding the Entity List Customer’s status as an Entity List party, our International Sanctions
Advisor is of the view that our historical transactions with the Entity List Customer are unlikely to have
involved ‘‘items subject to the EAR’’ or required U.S. export licences under the EAR.
Having considered (i) the limited scope of our historical business dealings involving U.S. export

U.S. Outbound Investment Rule
The Outbound Investment Rule
On October 28, 2024, the U.S. government issued the Provisions Pertaining to U.S. Investments in
Certain National Security Technologies and Products in Countries of Concern, codified at 31 C.F.R. part
850, to implement Executive Order 14105 dated August 9, 2023 (the ‘‘Outbound Investment Rule’’).
The Outbound Investment Rule took effect on January 2, 2025 and applies to transactions with a
completion date on or after that date.
The Outbound Investment Rule imposes prohibition and notification requirements on U.S. persons
for certain investments in persons of a country of concern, including entities organized under the laws
of, headquartered in, incorporated in, or with a principal place of business in China, Hong Kong or
Macau, that engage in certain covered activities relating to: (i) semiconductors and microelectronics, (ii)
quantum information technologies, and (iii) artificial intelligence systems, collectively referred to as
‘‘covered foreign persons.’’ Unless an exception applies, U.S. persons subject to the Outbound
Investment Rule are prohibited from making, or required to report, certain investments in covered
foreign persons, which are defined as ‘‘covered transactions.’’ Covered transactions include, among
others, acquisitions of equity interests that are not yet publicly traded, certain debt financing, joint
ventures, and certain investments as a limited partner in a non-U.S. person pooled investment fund,
subject to applicable exceptions and conditions.
The Outbound Investment Rule excepts from its coverage certain transactions, including
investments in publicly traded securities, denominated in any currency, that trade on a securities
exchange or over-the-counter in any jurisdiction, provided that such investments do not afford a U.S.
person rights beyond standard minority shareholder protections with respect to the covered foreign
person.
Impact of the Outbound Investment Rule on our Group
Our International Sanctions Advisor is of the view that the Outbound Investment Rule is not
expected to have a material adverse impact on our Group or the Global Offering because:
. We are persons of a country of concern under the Outbound Investment Rule, as our
Company is headquartered, incorporated and has its principal place of business in the PRC.
However, a person of a country of concern would constitute a covered foreign person only if
it engages in covered activities under the Outbound Investment Rule.
. Based on our business activities and product scope, we do not currently engage, and do not
plan to engage, in covered activities relating to semiconductors and microelectronics,
quantum information technologies or artificial intelligence systems. In particular, we are
principally engaged in the development and manufacture of tools, materials and equipment
used in PCB manufacturing and related precision machining processes. We do not design,
develop or produce equipment used for semiconductor advanced packaging, including
equipment supporting 2.5D or 3D integrated circuit assembly, through-silicon vias, die
bonding or heterogeneous integration. Our products and equipment are technologically and
functionally distinct from semiconductor advanced packaging equipment, such as lithography,
etching, bonding or chemical mechanical polishing systems.
– 167 –

=== PAGE 178 ===
BUSINESS
. Based on the above and as advised by our International Sanctions Advisor, we are unlikely to
constitute a covered foreign person under the Outbound Investment Rule. Accordingly, the
Outbound Investment Rule is not expected to impose prohibition or notification requirements
in respect of the subscription for or investment in our H Shares in the Global Offering. In
addition, the Outbound Investment Rule contains an exception for investments in publicly
traded securities, which further supports the view that the Outbound Investment Rule is not
expected to have a material adverse impact on our Group or the Global Offering after the
Listing.
Enhanced internal control measures relating to sanctions and export controls
To identify, assess and manage risks arising from applicable trade restrictions, tariff policies,
international sanctions and export controls, we have established, and will continue to enhance, a series
of internal control measures. In particular, we have adopted the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Monopoly
and Economic Sanctions Management Policy to govern our compliance framework in relation to
sanctions and export controls. We also plan to provide mandatory sanctions and export control
compliance training to our senior management and key personnel in our sales, finance, procurement and
legal functions.
In addition, upon entering into each contract with a customer, we will issue a notification letter
containing trade compliance and sanctions-related provisions, and we will require our suppliers to
provide compliance undertakings in relation to applicable trade restrictions, sanctions and export control
laws and regulations. We will also review and update our list of sensitive countries and regions at least
once every six months with reference to applicable sanctions and export control laws and regulations.
We also plan to integrate mandatory trade compliance screening into our supplier onboarding and
customer registration procedures through our Supplier Information Form and Customer Registration
Application. Our relevant business departments will continuously monitor our business partners and
promptly report any material changes to the relevant department heads and our legal department.
Furthermore, our internal audit department will conduct independent annual audits of our sanctions and
export control compliance framework, covering, among other matters, compliance in supplier
onboarding.
Having considered, among others, (i) the limited nature and value of our historical transactions
involving sanctions or export control considerations; (ii) the advice of our International Sanctions
Advisor that such transactions are unlikely to have involved violations of applicable primary sanctions
or U.S. export control laws and that the risk of such transactions constituting Secondary Sanctionable
Activities is likely remote; (iii) our remedial measures, including ceasing to place or accept new orders
with Sanctioned Targets or customers in Sanctioned Countries and winding down the relevant existing
transactions; and (iv) our enhanced internal control measures, including sanctions and export control
policies, counterparty screening, compliance undertakings, staff training, ongoing monitoring and
internal audits, our Directors are of the view, that our enhanced internal control measures relating to
sanctions and export controls are adequate and effective to identify, assess, manage and mitigate the
relevant compliance risks. Nothing has come to the Joint Sponsors’ attention that would disagree with
the Directors’ view above.

Data Collection. During the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, our
customers were principally corporate clients rather than individual customers. In the ordinary course of
our business operations, we primarily process only limited data necessary for contract negotiation, order
fulfilment, invoicing, logistics, after-sales service, and supplier management. We generally do not obtain

performance purposes.
Data Transmission. All data from our production bases in the Chinese Mainland is stored
domestically in the Chinese Mainland. For our overseas production bases, production site data is stored
locally, while certain operational and business data is stored in Chinese Mainland, and access to such
data is managed through secure connections and controlled permissions. We do not share or transfer data
collected by us to any third party without prior explicit consent. Without explicit consent, we prohibit
disclosing collected data to any third party unless mandated by a court or administrative order. During

no relevant data leakage incident in connection with the transfer of employee personal data by our
German Subsidiary to the Chinese Mainland.
Data Protection
To ensure the protection of our data and maintain the confidentiality of sensitive information, we
have implemented a robust set of security measures designed to prevent unauthorized access and
mitigate potential risks: (i) data encryption. We employ advanced encryption technologies to secure
sensitive business data both at rest and during transmission, preventing unauthorized access and
reducing the risk of data breaches; (ii) access control. Access to our data is strictly regulated, with
permissions granted only to authorized employees based on their roles and responsibilities. Sensitive
information is accessible only to those with the appropriate clearance, ensuring secure data handling;
(iii) physical access control. Entry to our facilities and networks is limited to authorized personnel.
Visitors must sign in upon arrival, and access to secure areas is tightly controlled, requiring prior
approval; and (iv) employee training. We provide ongoing data privacy and security training to all
employees, ensuring compliance with data protection policies and enhancing awareness of how to
securely handle sensitive information.
Information Security Framework
We established internal policies and a series of procedures for effective information and
cybersecurity management. Key of these internal policies and procedures include (i) network security, in
which we employ firewalls, antivirus software and intrusion detection systems to protect our network
infrastructure from external threats. Our network architecture features dual-link redundancy to ensure
stable and secure information transmission, (ii) data protection and privacy, in which we maintain a set
of protocols for data handling and storage, including encryption, access controls and regular data
backups, (iii) security audits and testing, in which we perform routine cybersecurity penetration testing
and vulnerability assessment to evaluate the robustness of our system, (iv) employee training, in which
we provide regular training programs to enhance overall security awareness, and (v) disaster recovery

According to Frost & Sullivan, the global PCB drilling tools industry is highly competitive and
relatively concentrated, with the top five drill bit manufacturers in the industry accounting for
approximately 75.7% of the total market share in terms of sales volume in 2025. We ranked first among

ESG Governance
We attach great importance to ESG governance and have established the ESG Management System
and an ESG governance structure consisting of the Board, the ESG Management Committee and the
ESG Working Group, with responsibilities of each level to integrate ESG concepts into corporate
operations and decision-making processes.
The Board, as the leadership and decision-making body for ESG work, is responsible for (i)
reviewing and approving the ESG governance system and approving the ESG report of the Company;
(ii) establishing the sustainability governance strategy, objectives and medium-to-long-term plans of the
Company; (iii) supervising and guiding the sustainable development work of the Company, identifying,
– 170 –

assessing and continuously monitoring material sustainability risks and opportunities, prioritizing
sustainability risks and opportunities to determine management priorities, thereby making effective risk
control decisions; and (iv) supervising the Company’s consideration of sustainable development-related
impacts, risks and opportunities when formulating major strategies and making major transaction
decisions.
The ESG Working Group is responsible for collecting and organizing ESG-related data arising
from the Group’s daily operations, as well as identifying potential ESG risks and opportunities. Such
information is consolidated and submitted to the ESG Management Committee for review.
Upon reviewing the aforementioned information, the ESG Management Committee reports the
Group’s ESG performance, key risks and recommendations for improvement to the Board on a regular
basis. While such reporting is generally conducted on an annual basis, management will provide ad hoc
reports to the Board as necessary in the event of ESG-related matters that may exert a material impact
on the Group’s operations or reputation.
We continue to strengthen internal ESG capabilities through training for employees at different
levels, including directors and senior management, and plan to continue such training and disclose
relevant goals and performance in our annual ESG report. In addition, the Company is committed to
promoting diversity on its Board, for details, please refer to ‘‘Directors and Senior Management —

Identification and Management of ESG Issues
The management of the Group has established a list of ESG issues based on its business model,

Indicators and Targets
Guided by China’s ‘‘Dual Carbon’’ goals (Carbon Peaking and Carbon Neutrality), we have
designated 2024 as our base year. Taking into account our business development plans, we have
established medium-to-long-term greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reduction targets and implementation
roadmaps. The Group intends to prioritize the gradual reduction of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions,
while exploring emission reduction measures for Scope 3 (Value Chain) where appropriate. These
targets will be implemented through a multi-pronged, phased approach and will be reviewed and
adjusted periodically in light of changes in the Group’s operating conditions, technological capabilities
and applicable regulatory requirements.
We are committed to continuously enhancing our environmental management. Adhering to the core
principles of ‘‘reduction, reuse, and detoxification,’’ we have implemented safeguard measures for
pollutant discharge, waste management and resource consumption. In alignment with the requirements of
the ESG Reporting Guide set out in the Listing Rules of the Stock Exchange, we will continue to refine
our ESG-related targets based on the following assumptions and our actual circumstances: (i) our
existing business scale and operational development expectations within a reasonable future period, (ii)
that there will be no material changes to applicable laws, regulations, and regulatory requirements in the
foreseeable future and (iii) that the Group can progressively allocate resources to improve ESG
performance without causing a material adverse effect on its normal operations.

Occupational Health and Safety
We are committed to creating a healthy and safe working environment for our employees, strictly
adhering to relevant occupational health and safety laws and regulations in our operating locations, and
formulating internal management policies to protect employee health and prevent workplace hazards. We
have passed the ISO 45001 Occupational Health and Safety Management System certification. During
the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, we had not experienced any fatalities due
to work safety accidents, nor have we paid any material claims or compensation to our employees in this
regard. Furthermore, we have not been subject to any material administrative penalties due to non-
compliance with applicable work safety laws and regulations.
Our principal occupational health and safety measures include employee training, regular
identification of workplace hazards and emergency drills, the Emergency Rescue Plan for Occupational
Disease Hazard Accidents and annual employee health check-ups.

We attach importance to talent development, providing employees with a sound training system

the Training Management System to establish a diversified employee training programs, which
efficiently integrate, organize, and utilize training resources, provide employees with a wide range of
training courses, and encourage employees to pursue further education, offering subsidies and rewards.

Social Insurance and Housing Provident Fund
Background
Pursuant to applicable PRC laws and regulations, we are required to make contributions to social
insurance and housing provident fund schemes for our employees in China. During the Track Record
Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, we made social insurance and housing provident fund
contributions for employees who had completed their probationary periods based on the minimum
contribution base required by the relevant local authorities. However, we did not make contributions in
full amount based on employees’ actual wages as required under PRC laws and regulations, nor did we
make social insurance and housing provident fund contributions for certain employees such as
employees during their probationary period or those who voluntarily choose not to have social insurance
and housing provident fund contributions made by the Company. The shortfall in social insurance and
housing provident fund contributions amounted to approximately RMB27.1 million, RMB40.1 million
and RMB40.7 million in 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively.
Such shortfalls were primarily attributable to (i) certain employees’ preference not to make social
insurance and housing provident fund contributions based on their actual wages, as this would increase
the corresponding employee contribution portion, (ii) certain employees’ preference not to make social
insurance and housing provident fund contributions through the Company, as they had already
participated in such schemes in other regions; and (iii) our historical practice of making such
contributions based on the minimum contribution base required by the relevant local authorities and not
making such contributions during probationary periods.
Potential Legal Consequences
According to our PRC Legal Advisor, under the Social Insurance Law of the People’s Republic of
China (2018 Revision), where an employer fails to pay social insurance premiums in full and on time,
the social insurance collection authority may order it to make payment or make up the arrears within a
prescribed time limit and impose a late payment surcharge at a rate of 0.05% per day on the outstanding
amount from the date of default. If the employer fails to make such payment within the prescribed
period, the relevant administrative authority may impose a fine ranging from one to three times the
amount in arrears. In addition, pursuant to the Regulations on the Administration of Housing Provident
Fund (2019 Revision), where an employer fails to pay or underpays housing provident fund
contributions, the competent housing provident fund administration center may order it to make up such
contributions within a prescribed time limit and may apply to a people’s court for compulsory
enforcement if the employer fails to comply.
– 178 –

=== PAGE 189 ===
BUSINESS
Pursuant to the Interpretation (II) of the Supreme People’s Court on Issues Concerning the
Application of Law in the Trial of Labor Dispute Cases (the ‘‘Judicial Interpretation (II)’’), any
agreement between an employer and an employee to waive statutory social insurance contributions shall
be deemed invalid. As advised by our PRC Legal Advisor, the statutory obligation of employers to
participate in social insurance and make contributions in accordance with applicable laws and
regulations existed prior to the issuance of Judicial Interpretation (II), and there have been no material
changes to the applicable contribution policies before and after its issuance.
As of the Latest Practicable Date, (i) we had not been subject to any material administrative
penalties in relation to insufficient contributions to social insurance or housing provident fund; (ii) we
had not received any material complaints or reports from employees in this regard; (iii) we had not
received any notices from relevant authorities requiring us to make supplementary contributions, conduct
investigations or accept penalties; and (iv) we had not encountered any material disagreements with the
relevant authorities in connection with such matters.
As advised by our PRC Legal Advisor, on the premise that there are no material changes to the
current policies and regulations governing social insurance and housing provident fund contributions and
that no employee complaints, reports, litigation or arbitration are initiated, the risk that the competent
authorities would initiate comprehensive and concentrated recovery of the aforesaid historical shortfalls
and impose material administrative penalties is remote.
In light of the foregoing, including (i) the absence of material disputes or penalties, (ii) the
absence of rectification or payment notices from competent authorities, and (iii) the advice of our PRC
Legal Advisor as to the remote likelihood of retrospective recovery or material penalties, our Directors
are of the view that the historical non-compliance relating to social insurance and housing provident
fund contributions is unlikely to have, and will not have, a material adverse effect on our business,
financial condition or results of operations. As a result, we had not made any provision for the shortfall
in our social insurance and housing provident fund contributions during the Track Record Period.
Remedial Measures and Internal Control Measures
As of the Latest Practicable Date, we and our domestic subsidiaries had made social insurance and
housing provident fund contributions for new employees who were then in their probationary periods.
To improve compliance with social insurance and housing provident fund contribution
requirements and to prevent recurrence of similar matters, we have implemented the following internal
control measures: (i) We have adopted a Remuneration Management Policy, which requires
contributions to social insurance and housing provident fund in accordance with applicable national and
local regulations. (ii) We have established approval procedures under which the Human Resources
Department prepares and submits payment requests. (iii) We provide training to our human resources
personnel on relevant legal and regulatory requirements relating to social insurance and housing
provident fund contributions. We monitor regulatory developments relating to social insurance and
housing provident fund policies on an ongoing basis.
Our Directors consider that the implemented rectification measures are adequate and effective, as
evidenced by the clear delineation of internal responsibilities, the enhancement of the control and
compliance environment, and the proactive measures in mitigating risks of recurring contribution
shortfalls.

Non-registration of Lease Agreements
As of December 31, 2025, all of our lease agreements in the PRC had not been registered with
relevant authorities. As the registration of a lease agreement requires the cooperation between the lessor
and lessee and lessors are typically unwilling to undertake the administrative burden due to the low risk
of penalty, we were not able to complete the registration of lease agreements mentioned above. We have
adopted internal policies that (i) request our employees to proactively coordinate with lessors to
complete the registration for all of our lease agreements; and (ii) require our employees to complete the
registration of lease agreements in instances in which lessors are willing to cooperate in such
procedures.
